items.quote: it is repugnant neither to Nature nor Reason that a Man may prolong his life beyond the common ordinary age of Men, even to a long time
items.note: Croll holds that life can be lengthened beyond the ordinary age, against those who call this vain talk.

items.quote: and that for two Reasons
items.note: Announces a numbered pair of reasons; the first opens CH6.70, the second CH6.71.

items.quote: Tis possible to extend a long life farther
items.note: The margin restates the claim of CH6.69 as a heading.

items.name: Porta
items.quote: Therefore Porta reject the opinion of those that cast mens fortune from the day or houre of their nativity prefixing the bounds of life
items.note: Porta is named beside CH6.69 as rejecting a fixed term of life read from the hour of birth.

items.name: Parac.
items.quote: Parac. chap. 7. of the Labyrinth of Physitians
items.note: A writing of Paracelsus is named beside CH6.69, evidence of whose view stands there.

items.quote: in NATURALS there is no certaine appointed Terme apparent what day we shall die, but it is in our own hand and power to put an end to our life if we will
items.note: First reason: in natural things no day of death is fixed; ending or prolonging life lies in our power.

items.quote: I speak here Phylosophically of the Naturall death
items.note: Croll tells the reader in which sense his words are meant: philosophically, not theologically.

items.quote: the Naturall death, which is onely the wasting of the Naturall Moysture and Heat, as may be seen in a burning lamp
items.note: Natural death is defined as the wasting of natural moisture and heat, likened to a lamp burning out.

items.quote: not Theologically of the Fatall death and utmost Terme which God hath prefixt to every one
items.note: The fatal death is the utmost term God has set for each person, set apart from natural death.

items.quote: Death is the Bound which we cannot passe, nor is there any day or hour, for by the Grace of God we live the Terme without houres
items.note: Death is a bound that cannot be passed, yet no day or hour of it is fixed.

items.quote: As God hath numbred our hairs, so also doth he reckon our years, leaving them in our power
items.note: God counts our years but leaves them in our power.

items.quote: a long and lasting life of Man in this world is not displeasing to him, especially if it be spent in the Fear and Service of his Creator
items.note: A long life is said to please God, chiefly when spent in his service.

items.quote: that utmost and fixed Terme or determined poynt of DIVINE PREDESTINATION which is unknown to mortalls
items.note: The final term set by God is said to be unknown to men; no one can go beyond it.

items.quote: so may he prolong his life by removing these impediments, so that at last he may attaine to the appointed Terme of the Nature of life
items.note: Diseases shorten life; removing them lets a man reach the term nature appointed.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: See Paracelsus of long life
items.note: A writing of Paracelsus is named beside the passage on the fixed term of life.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: See Paracelsus in lib. 8
items.note: Paracelsus is named beside the bound no man can pass.

items.name: Archid.
items.quote: Archid. of the Elixirs
items.note: A writing named Archid. of the Elixirs stands beside the passage on diseases shortening life; the lines after it may be drawn from it.

items.quote: It is the conservation of the Human body from all accidentall corruption
items.note: Standing right after the naming of the Elixirs, this seems to say what an elixir is; the note does not show plainly what It refers to.

items.quote: Death Gods minister expecteth our intestine war
items.note: Death is pictured as God's minister waiting on a war within us; a figurative phrase.

items.quote: There is a two fold death, from the Iliad or first principle, and from the Ens or Being
items.note: Two kinds of death are set apart by their source: the Iliad and the Ens.

items.quote: from the Iliad or first principle
items.note: Iliad is glossed as first principle.

items.quote: from the Ens or Being
items.note: Ens is glossed as Being.

items.quote: The Soule of perpetuity or the Spirit of Light joyned to Nature with the light is perpetuall
items.note: The Soul of perpetuity is equated with the Spirit of Light; joined to nature it is perpetual and will not let such a life be short.

items.quote: God hath created the aforesaid Medicine for the preservation of life
items.note: Second reason; points back to a medicine named earlier in the text, not in the lines given.

items.quote: which may preserve our body as well from the corruption of our Parents, as from the defect of our own government, cure its infirmities, and repaire what is wasted
items.note: What the medicine does: preserves from inherited corruption and from bad living, cures, restores.

items.quote: ultimate death the most Terrible of all Terrible things (which is the destruction of the Mummy)
items.note: Ultimate death is defined as the destruction of the Mummy, ordained by God as the wages of sinners.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: Paracelsus saith that the death which is from the resolution of the Iliad may be hindred by the industry of the Physitian, but that which is from the Ens or Being cannot
items.note: Paracelsus is given as saying death from the Iliad can be hindered by a physician, death from the Ens cannot.

items.quote: as we may preserve a little fire by laying on more wood; so also may our life be prolonged by administring such Remedies and secrets
items.note: Life is likened to a fire and remedies to wood laid on it.

items.quote: we being destitute of wisdome know not that wood wherewith our life might be cherished and prolonged
items.note: The word wood is carried over from the simile to stand for the unknown remedy.

items.quote: not by Nature and property of Time, for then all had been Long-liv'd, but by the help of Secrets
items.note: Adam and men of his time lived long not by nature but by secrets and wisdom.

items.quote: by Wisdome which was revealed but to few, and by speciall knowledge which God gave them in this particular
items.note: The wisdom of long life was revealed only to a few.

items.quote: Many holy men used this universall Medicine before the flood
items.note: The medicine is named universal and said to have been used before the flood.

items.name: Lactantius
items.quote: which Adam also had in his Family, as Lactantius witnesseth
items.note: Lactantius is cited for Adam having the medicine in his family.

items.quote: which strengthneth the Internall Balsom, and like Fire congregateth Homogeneous things, and segregateth Heterogeneous
items.note: What the medicine works: strengthens the internal balsam, gathers like things and separates unlike, as fire does.

items.quote: Nor are we to relie upon their judgements, who being ignorant of the Mysteries of the Element of Water, dream that the Deluge washed away the efficacy of fruits
items.note: Croll rejects the view that the flood weakened plants or men's bodies; he ties it to ignorance of the mysteries of water.

items.quote: Wherefore we want nothing but the knowledge of Secrets, and their use
items.note: All that is lacking is the knowledge and use of secrets.

items.quote: the Flood did not wast the things that grow, but wash'd away our wisdome of knowing them
items.note: What the flood took away was knowledge, not the power of growing things.

items.quote: These most secret of secrets have ever been hid from the common sort of them that professe Phylosophy
items.note: These secrets have always been hidden from the common sort of philosophers, especially since wisdom began to be abused.

items.quote: wise men lived together in the Centre reserving wisdome among themselves, but banished those that had it not into the circumference
items.note: The wise kept wisdom among themselves and put the rest outside.

items.name: Paracels.
items.quote: Paracels.
items.note: The note on the wise in the Centre is signed with Paracelsus's name.

items.quote: as few reach the Naturall Terme, so also few have known the reason of prolonging the life
items.note: Few reach the natural term and few know how to prolong life.

items.quote: the life is broken off, or shortned, two manner of wayes
items.note: Announces two ways life is shortened; the first in CH6.73, the second in CH6.74.

items.quote: MENS & ENS abrumpunt nobis vitam
items.note: The margin names the two causes that break off life: mind and being.

items.quote: by the MIND, whence arise mentall diseases which are invisible, and affect us in our Mind
items.note: Mental diseases are those arising from the mind, invisible, affecting the mind.

items.quote: as Inchantment, Imagination, Estimation, Influence; Superstition, all which proceed from a spirituall affection
items.note: Five mental diseases are listed, all from a spiritual affection.

items.quote: No corporall guard or shelter availeth any thing against such like violences, but onely Faith which is able to resist them
items.note: Only faith, not bodily means, resists these diseases.

items.quote: some other Magicall means is requisite against witchcrafts and to cure those that are bewitched, and though the cure be difficult, yet is it possible
items.note: Magical means are also needed against witchcraft; the cure is hard but possible.

items.quote: Notwithstanding what may be said, i. e. that the act of the imagination is immanent, and that one mans body cannot be altered by another mans imagination
items.note: An objection is set aside: that imagination acts only within and cannot alter another's body.

items.quote: these diseases which only Adept Physitians know, are healed without the help of Natural Physick
items.note: Only adept physicians know these diseases; they are healed without natural physic.

items.quote: in the minds of men there is a kind of a hidden Virtue, of changing, attracting, and binding that which it desireth
items.note: The mind has a hidden power to change, attract and bind, strongest with imagination and will.

items.quote: the Antipathicall Loadstone, which doth (as it were) bewitch spiritually and invisibly
items.note: The loadstone is said to bewitch only as it were: the text marks its own comparison as not plain.

items.quote: these five supernatural mischiefs
items.note: The five mental diseases are counted and named supernatural mischiefs.

items.quote: i. e. Inchantment, Imagination, Estimation, Influence, Superstition
items.note: The margin says what the five mischiefs are.

items.quote: their malignant Astra's must be averted by a supernaturall cure and magicall help into something else, without any prophanation of Gods Name
items.note: The cure: their malignant astra are turned aside into something else by supernatural and magical help.

items.quote: Thus those diseases that proceed from the Mind require a mentall cure
items.note: Diseases of the mind need a cure of the mind.

items.name: Paracels.
items.quote: of which see more in Paracels. his Philosophia Sagaci
items.note: A writing of Paracelsus is named for more on the mental cure.

items.quote: Godlinesse is the chiefest remedy, guard, and preservation against such like evills
items.note: Godliness is the chief remedy against these evils.

items.quote: by the Being, as by Entall or Corporall diseases
items.note: The second way life is shortened: by the Being, that is by entall or bodily diseases.

items.quote: Health is preserved by fastings, and a moderate Diet is the best Governance to prolong the life
items.note: Fasting and moderate diet preserve health; gluttony has killed many.

items.quote: is to be sought from Natural causes and means, to wit, from the Elements and hidden Secrets
items.note: Bodily harms from the Ens are to be cured by natural means, from the elements and hidden secrets.

items.quote: Corporall medicines doe no good to mentall or supernaturall distempers, nor can mentall medicines be profitable to bodily diseases
items.note: Each kind of disease needs its own kind of cure.

items.name: Theophrastus
items.quote: as Theophrastus in his Books very often observeth
items.note: Theophrastus is cited for the many accidents, from the womb onward, that keep men from the natural term.

items.quote: wander wider then the bounds of a Preface, I shall now draw to a conclusion
items.note: Croll names the writing a Preface and announces its conclusion.

items.quote: though divine Misteries are far greater than to be set forth by the splendor of mans words
items.note: Divine mysteries exceed what words can set forth.

items.quote: I have inserted in their proper places in this Prolix and Admonitory Preface
items.note: Points to the whole Preface as the place where his gains are set down, each in its proper place.

items.quote: so far as was lawfull, and so much as was allowable by God, have I imparted candidly from the intimate and inmost Armory or Treasury of my Heart
items.note: He imparted only as much as was lawful and allowed by God.

items.quote: to the Children of Learning and Heirs of Wisdome, who with second thoughts which are the wisest
items.note: The Preface is addressed to a named class of readers.

items.quote: reading them over in the light of God, without any superfluity or diminution, by often reiterated and evident speculations
items.note: Readers are told to read repeatedly, adding and taking away nothing.

items.quote: Read them over and over, & over again, and againe; I hope it shall not repent thee of thy paines
items.note: The margin urges reading again and again.

items.quote: it concerns the publick good to make known also in publick writing what belongs to the publick
items.note: Knowledge that belongs to the public should be made known in writing.

items.quote: We ought not to prefer our private profit before the publick good
items.note: The margin states the duty to the public good.

items.quote: I see it taught in publick Schools for the most part rather for the glory of Education, than the good and profit of the Auditors
items.note: Croll faults the public schools of his time.

items.quote: The School of Physick is not covered with tile, but with the Firmament
items.note: The school of physic is pictured as roofed by the sky, not a building.

items.quote: in that of ESNE at Lyons in France, and in that of BAPPENHEIMIE in the Segniory of Mareschall
items.what: two of the very best and most honourable Families
items.note: Names the two families with whom he lived over ten years, which gave him access to learned men.

items.quote: that Physitian that walketh according to the mind of Paracelsus is onely able to open the Book of Nature
items.note: Only a physician following Paracelsus can open the Book of Nature.

items.quote: the BOOK of NATURE (in which every region is a leaf)
items.note: The Book of Nature is glossed: every region is one of its leaves, read by travel.

items.quote: not profunctorily & superficially, but practically and experimentally
items.note: Nature is to be studied by practice and experiment.

items.quote: Heroick Prince CHRISTIAN ANHALTIN, with his more then singular favor and laudable patronage toward the more secret Studies
items.note: Names his patron and calls the field the more secret studies.

items.quote: all these Medicins come to, which must be prepar'd and try'd by Fire
items.note: The medicines are prepared and tested by fire, at great cost.

items.quote: It will be safe for every man to add hereunto the further Experiences of his own, and dispose it otherwise according to his discretion for his private use
items.note: The order of medicaments is his own; readers may add and rearrange.

items.quote: this harvest of Chymicall Corn, and the First fruits of my increase, and this Spagyrick present of my difficult and laborious diligence
items.note: Croll names his work as a harvest, first fruits and a spagyric present.

items.quote: for I regard not Hogs & Dogs that have no grace nor goodnes at all
items.note: Unworthy readers are excluded from those he writes for.

items.quote: who have been train'd up in the Spagyrick and Hermetick School of Vulcan, being not yet deprived of the Light of understanding
items.note: The work is meant above all for those trained in the spagyric school.

items.quote: I have not handled all things here in this place, to avoyd prolixity; I know there are not a few doubts left unresolved
items.note: He says things are left out and doubts left open.

items.quote: It is provided for by the Philosophical law that some tedious things should be left obscure to young Schollers and for intelligent & wise men to find out
items.note: Some things are left obscure on purpose, for the wise to find out and to test their wits.

items.quote: He that can receive it let him receive it; and he that doth not understand, let him either learn or hold his peace and be silent
items.note: The text is for those able to receive it.

items.quote: he may apprehend & conjecture the signification of MANY things by a Few in this open market of Nature
items.note: The diligent reader is told to infer many things from few.

items.quote: the doors and Inner rooms are unlockt to him by the favorable virtue of the most high Creator
items.note: Inner rooms are unlocked to the right reader by God; the rest stays shut.

items.quote: through PRAYER & PAINS, shall reap much more fruit than he expected
items.note: Understanding comes through prayer and labour.

items.quote: I have not spoken of so many things, but there yet more left to be spaken
items.note: More is left unsaid.

items.quote: These things are writen for them who by aprospicocious & happy wit have their mind inlightned by God
items.note: The writing is meant for readers enlightened by God.

items.quote: A few things or words are sufficient for him that understandeth
items.note: Few words suffice for one who understands.

items.quote: to get the corn from the chaffe, and separate true from false, is sometime a most tedious and difficult task
items.note: Against critics who call the work a mixture of good and bad, he says sorting true from false is hard.

items.quote: let them take their lited candle from under the bushel, lest the curse of the figtree befall them
items.note: Critics are told to publish their own observations.

items.name: Mat.
items.note: A chapter of Matthew is named beside the curse of the fig tree.

items.quote: whose purpose is not to find out that which is True but to wrangle about it
items.note: He rejects the contentious sceptic philosopher.

items.quote: for surely Physick is not yet come to the Limit of perfection, but many things remain to be discovered to future ages
items.note: Physic is unfinished; more is left for later ages.

items.quote: For who can find out the end of Physick
items.note: The margin says physic has no reachable end.

items.quote: to succor poor Lazarus, not wth Sylogistical or Levitical Words, but with a Samaritan Help & Ayd
items.note: The sick are figured as Lazarus; help is to be in deeds, not words.

items.quote: conspire together with us into an union and Spagyrick mellifice divorcing the multitude and abstaining from all fornication
items.note: Critics may become bees and join a spagyric honey-making; the bee figure carries a second sense of a union apart from the multitude.

items.quote: after other secret Sciences which yet lie in the dark
items.note: Other secret sciences are said to lie in the dark still.

items.quote: that Ancient, True, & Philosophical Medicin
items.note: The medicine is named once more at the close, said to be not yet fully known.

items.quote: may in a shorttime by the heavenly assistance, be restored to its lost lustre & ancient splendor
items.note: He expects the ancient medicine to be restored soon.

items.quote: some tedious things should be left obscure to young Schollers and for intelligent & wise men to find out
items.note: Within the same paragraph he says knowledge for the public must be made known in public writing, and that some things are left obscure on purpose; the lines given do not show how he joins the two.

items.quote: Which that holy Triunity grant, whose unspeakable Name be blessed for ever and ever
items.note: Closing prayer to the Trinity.

items.quote: AMEN
items.note: The Preface ends.
